blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — aseptic urinary-catheter insertion and maintenance of a closed drainage system
stem: An indwelling urinary catheter is being inserted in an acute-care hospital. Which technique best reflects current CDC CAUTI-prevention guidance?

options.A: Use hand hygiene before/after insertion, aseptic technique, sterile gloves/equipment, a single-use lubricant packet, and a closed drainage system.
options.B: Perform hand hygiene and use sterile gloves and catheter equipment, but use lubricant from a shared clean container before connecting a closed drainage system.
options.C: Perform hand hygiene and use a sterile catheter kit with clean gloves, changing to sterile gloves only after insertion before connecting the drainage system.
options.D: Perform hand hygiene and use sterile insertion equipment, then disconnect the catheter from the drainage tubing after urine return to verify flow before reconnecting.

rationale: A is correct. Current CDC CAUTI recommendations state that hand hygiene should be performed immediately before and after catheter insertion or manipulation and that, in the acute-care hospital setting, urinary catheters should be inserted using aseptic technique and sterile equipment. CDC specifically lists sterile gloves, drape and sponges, an appropriate antiseptic or sterile solution for periurethral cleaning, and a single-use packet of lubricant jelly. After aseptic insertion, a closed drainage system should be maintained. B is incorrect because CDC specifies a single-use lubricant packet rather than a shared lubricant container. C is incorrect because acute-care insertion requires sterile gloves during the insertion procedure, not clean gloves with sterile gloves added only afterward. D is incorrect because intentional disconnection compromises the closed system; CDC states that if disconnection, leakage, or a break in aseptic technique occurs, the catheter and collecting system should be replaced using aseptic technique and sterile equipment.
educational_objective: Prevent CAUTI during acute-care indwelling urinary-catheter insertion by using hand hygiene before and after insertion, aseptic technique, sterile equipment and sterile gloves, a single-use lubricant packet, and subsequent maintenance of a closed drainage system.
source_organization: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC); National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
source_document_title: Summary of Recommendations — Guideline for Prevention of Catheter-Associated Urinary Tract Infections; 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan
source_version_date: CDC CAUTI Summary of Recommendations page dated 2024-03-25 and current when rechecked 2026-08-20; 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan effective April 2026
source_locator: CDC CAUTI Summary of Recommendations lines 94-110, Proper Techniques for Urinary Catheter Insertion: II.A hand hygiene immediately before and after insertion/manipulation; II.C in acute-care hospitals insert using aseptic technique and sterile equipment; II.C.1 use sterile gloves, drape, sponges, appropriate antiseptic or sterile solution for periurethral cleaning, and a single-use lubricant-jelly packet. Lines 111-117, Proper Techniques for Urinary Catheter Maintenance: following aseptic insertion maintain a closed drainage system; if a break in aseptic technique, disconnection, or leakage occurs, replace the catheter and collecting system using aseptic technique and sterile equipment. NCSBN 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan Safety and Infection Prevention and Control page was visually verified earlier in this continuation and supports applying infection-prevention principles and appropriate safety/PPE procedures.
source_claim_supported: Fresh current CDC HTML directly supports every clinical element in the key: hand hygiene before and after insertion, aseptic acute-care insertion, sterile gloves/equipment, a single-use lubricant packet, and maintenance of a closed drainage system. It also directly supports rejecting intentional disconnection and clean-glove insertion in the acute-care setting. NCSBN supports the infection-prevention blueprint construct.

correction_summary: Original Q0116 contained absolute-word distractors and obvious clean-versus-sterile caricatures. The item was rebuilt so each distractor preserves some correct CAUTI-prevention elements while introducing one specific error: shared lubricant, clean gloves during insertion, or intentional system disconnection. Post-fetch review then made the CDC-required before-and-after hand-hygiene timing explicit in the key without creating a length cue.

option_audit.A: Correct; directly matches CDC hand hygiene before/after insertion, acute-care aseptic insertion, sterile gloves/equipment, single-use lubricant, and closed-system maintenance recommendations.
option_audit.B: Plausible near-correct technique; incorrect because CDC specifically recommends a single-use lubricant packet rather than a shared clean container.
option_audit.C: Plausible sterile-kit shortcut; incorrect because acute-care catheter insertion requires sterile gloves during insertion, not clean gloves followed by a later glove change.
option_audit.D: Plausible patency-check shortcut; incorrect because intentional disconnection breaks the closed system and CDC directs replacement after disconnection or another break in asepsis.

cueing_audit.absolute_words: No option relies on all/only/always/never/must/completely-type absolute wording.
cueing_audit.answer_length: Final option lengths: A 146, B 159, C 157, D 166 characters; the correct answer is the shortest, but all choices contain comparable multi-element technique descriptions and there is no positive-length cue.
cueing_audit.grammatical_lexical: All four alternatives begin with appropriate infection-prevention actions and differ by one clinically meaningful insertion or maintenance detail rather than obvious tone.
cueing_audit.second_answer_risk: No defensible second answer identified after refinement. B conflicts with the single-use lubricant recommendation, C conflicts with sterile-glove insertion requirements, and D intentionally breaks the closed system. Independent post-fetch reread remains required.
